entry.content:
Don't get confused: There is a 1987 film called Wings Of Desire, a British indie rock duo named Wings Of Desire, and now a Mia Joy single titled "Wings Of Desire." The song is what we're talking about today, as it's the dreamy lead single of her just-announced sophomore album Star Echo Heavy Dove.

Star Echo Heavy Dove is the long-awaited followup to her sprawling 2021 debut, Spirit Tamer. The Chicago musician returned with "Comet" last month, which features Peel Dream Magazine. That track isn't on the record, but there is one guest on the LP: Midwife, whose brand of spacey ambient is completely compatible with Joy's entrancing sound.

"Wings Of Desire" is inspired by the movie of the same title, and here's what Joy says about:

Seeing Wenders' film for the first time helped me move internal static to words — one of those seminal moments in life where what you're watching mirrors life so dearly my only way to resolve myself was to write this song. I'm gravitated to lonely characters, solitude, longing. One of Star Echo Heavy Dove's motifs is centered around balancing the tug of war between feeling satisfaction with being self-sufficient and the willingness to give that up for the vulnerability of expanding desire. There's a great message in there about living for all that life offers, letting yourself go even if you end up bleeding. 

Dive into the mesmeric tune below.

entry.title: Macklemore Kicks Off Free Palestine Tour With Hozier, Kneecap, & Ed Sheeran’s Backing Band

entry.content:
Last month, Ed Sheeran dropped Macklemore as the opener of his US stadium tour — reportedly because of pressure from Patriots owner Robert Kraft, who doesn't approve of Macklemore's stance against Israel's genocide of Palestinian people. Naturally, the resulted in a huge and justified backlash against Sheeran. All of Sheeran's other openers quit the tour, as did Beoga, the Irish folk band who backed him up during part of his show. Sheeran claimed that he's "not complicit" and then made a tearful but meaningless speech once his tour resumed. Meanwhile, Sheeran's shows at Kraft's Gillette Stadium were canceled for severe weather anyway, and then Zach Bryan wore a "Free Palestine" shirt while playing the same stadium. In the meantime, Macklemore announced his Free Palestine benefit tour, and he kicked it off with some surprise guests Monday night in Dublin.

Macklemore already announced that he's donating the $1 million that he earned as an Ed Sheeran opener to Palestinian aid, then said that all the protests from his Free Palestine tour will support the same cause. He assembled the tour quickly, only announcing three shows at the beginning but promising more to come. The first of those shows was last night at Dublin's sold-out 3Arena. The evening was billed as "Macklemore and Friends," and none of the friends were announced ahead of time. When it went down last night, Macklemore's guests included the Irish pop-folk star Hozier, the staunchly pro-Palestine Dublin rap group Kneecap, and the former Ed Sheeran backing band Beoga.

Billboard reports that other guests included dead prez member M1, singer-songwriter Lina Makoul, and DJ Habibeats, as well as appearances from regular Macklemore collaborators like Australian singer Tones & I and "Same Love" guest Mary Lambert. Game Of Thrones star Liam Cunningham and activists Nadia Greenspan and Samir Eskand spoke to the crowd, and the show had remote appearances from the Strokes' Julian Casablancas, Mark Ruffalo, Cynthia Nixon, Ilana Glazer, and Natasha Rothwell.

A member of Beoga told the crowd, "You don't fuck with the Irish" and that "the tide is changing."

Hozier's set included a performance of the Irish folk ballad "The Prayer Of Shields," which Hozier reportedly learned from Lankum's Ian Lynch, and a screen behind him showed a QR code that took people to a petition for Ireland to expedite the process for 55 Palestinian students whose scholarships have been approved but who are still awaiting visas from the Irish government.

Kneecap's set naturally included a whole lot of passionate talk about Irish solidarity and the importance of a free Palestine, and one of them told the crowd, "We’d like to thank Ed Sheeran for organizing this concert."

During his set, Macklemore said that his entire campaign started with "two words" — free Palestine — and that "those two words are so threatening to some people. They would rather silence those two words than confront what they actually mean. Because freedom that requires another person’s oppression is not freedom at all." He performed all his big hits, as well as his recent protest songs.

The remaining London and Paris dates on the Free Palestine tour are sold out, too. The Paris show goes down 10/29 at Accor Arena.

entry.title: Neil Young Sues Trump PAC Over “Rockin’ In The Free World”
entry.summary: Donald Trump just won’t stop using the Neil Young song “Rockin’ In The Free World” as entrance music at his rallies. As you might imagine, Young is not thrilled about this. Time and again, Young has made his disgust for Trump clear in protest songs and open letters. In 2020, Young sued Trump for his…
entry.content:
Donald Trump just won't stop using the Neil Young song "Rockin' In The Free World" as entrance music at his rallies. As you might imagine, Young is not thrilled about this. Time and again, Young has made his disgust for Trump clear in protest songs and open letters. In 2020, Young sued Trump for his use of the song, and that suit was settled out of court. Now, Young is suing Trump again, claiming that Trump has violated the settlement by continuing to use the song.

As Rolling Stone reports, lawyers for Neil Young have filed a $10 million copyright infringement lawsuit against Donald Trump's political action committee Trump 47 Committee Inc. in Virginia, where the PAC is based. The lawsuit doesn't personally name Trump himself as a defendant.

In their five-page filing, Young's lawyers write that the song "is the opposite of everything that Donald J. Trump stands for" and that Trump was "personally aware that a license would be required" for the song's usage. Young's lawyers claim taht Trump entered to "Rockin' In The Free World" at a midterm rally in Youngstown, Ohio Oct. 12.

The Brooklyn band makes a charming blend of indie rock and jangle pop, and they've opened for acts like the Pains Of Being Pure At Heart and Heavenly. If you don't like them yet, today's terrific track "If Not Soon Then Now" should win you over.

Trinket is the project of Madison Kate Proffitt and Sean Camargo, who are also involved in other groups: Proffitt plays in Lightheaded and Betty Brite, while Camargo leads the post-punk band S.C.A.B. Here's what they say of the highly infectious "If Not Soon Then Now":

This song is very directly about starting a relationship with someone new; it's exciting, but you quickly realize that insecurities, fears, and things you've dealt with in past relationships don't go away just because you've started over. It's also about having something that you're excited about and are scared you’re going to ruin it with those insecurities. It's almost like just the fear of it makes your worries come true.

Their debut LP is slated for next year. For now, check out "If Not Soon Then Now" below.

entry.content:
For the past decade, Sufjan Stevens has not been a touring artist. After wrapping up his travels supporting Carrie & Lowell in 2016, Stevens gave two live performances in 2017 and two more in 2018, including his Oscars appearance. He hadn't been onstage again until last month. In the interim, he released six full-length albums, including the "proper" Sufjan LPs The Ascension and Javelin and various collaborative efforts and side projects. There was also a global pandemic, the death of his partner Evans Richardson, and a battle with Guillain-Barré Syndrome that left him learning to walk again.

Since going public with his grief and his health struggles, Stevens has been easing his way back into public life with behind-the-scenes work, including producing John Legend's Christmas album and guest spots for various indie artists. His live return occurred Sept. 25 at Tempo in Kingston, NY, where he provided piano and vocals at Meg Lui's album release show. Stevens produced Lui's new album Instant Validation, a project that brought together lots of talented folks from their Hudson Valley friend group. People on r/sufjan noticed at the time of the gig, but the news has been circulating broadly more recently on social media.

News of Stevens' return to the stage comes just before next week's release of Worst Christmas Ever!, a new album paring his extensive catalog of Christmas music down to one disc. Out Nov. 6, it includes the new song "On This Christmas (It Only Gets Better)," his first new Christmas song in 15 years. "On this Christmas, I ask forgiveness for all the funny things I’ve said and done," he explained of the track in a press release.

entry.title: Jay-Z Confirmed For Super Bowl 2027 Halftime Show
entry.summary: Last week, a number of sources reported that Jay-Z had effectively selected himself as the headliner for next year’s Super Bowl Halftime Show. Jay’s company Roc Nation has produced every Halftime Show since 2020, so Jay effectively selected himself here. The reaction to the news of Jay as headliner has not been unanimously positive, but…
entry.content:
Last week, a number of sources reported that Jay-Z had effectively selected himself as the headliner for next year's Super Bowl Halftime Show. Jay's company Roc Nation has produced every Halftime Show since 2020, so Jay effectively selected himself here. The reaction to the news of Jay as headliner has not been unanimously positive, but any backlash wasn't enough to prevent the inevitable. Today, the NFL has confirmed it: Jay-Z is going to the Super Bowl.

An extremely brief teaser video has Jay-Z, filmed in crisp black and white, sitting in an empty stadium and scowling in the general direction of the camera as Just Blaze's piano notes from "Public Service Announcement (Interlude)" ring out. A message appears oncreen: "The GOAT's out of the bag."

As NPR reports, NFL commissioner Roger Goodell claims that he had one request when the league made the production deal with Roc Nation: He wanted Jay to perform at the Super Bowl "whenever the moment felt right to him." In a statement, Jay says, "From Reasonable Doubt to standing on the Super Bowl halftime stage, this has been a journey. Thirty years of music, work, and culture on the world's biggest stage. This run continues to be a dream come true."

The Super Bowl is coming to SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California Feb. 14. Jay-Z headlined two shows at the same venue last weekend, bringing in many special guests and dismissing reports of soft ticket sales as AI "tricknology." Jay has returned to the stage in a series of stadium shows this year, and he's also cut off his dreadlocks, switching things up so that he'll once again look like the classic version of himself, which feels like it was all leading up to this announcement.

At this point, Jay-Z has been semi-retired from music for nearly a decade — much longer than the period of time in which he supposedly actually retired after The Black Album. His Halftime Show will follow those from Kendrick Lamar and Bad Bunny, two artists who were having tremendous zeitgeist moments in their respective years. Jay can't claim anything like that, and his booking feels like more of a classic Super Bowl nostalgia move, like all those years when the Rolling Stones or Tom Petty or the Who would play the big show.

My colleague Chris DeVille got a lot of pushback last week for noting that Jay is a great live performer with a ton of hits, but that's the truth! I've seen Jay live many times, and when he's got a crowd of his fans rocking with him, he is tremendous. (Or at least he was tremendous; it's probably been 15 years since I've seen him live.) But Jay doesn't have a lot of experience with the kind of overwhelming, heavily choreographed 15-minute spectacle that the Halftime Show has become, and we'll just have to see whether he's up to it.

entry.title: Dead Man’s Bones Share “Lost In The Night,” First New Music In 17 Years
entry.summary: A glorious time is upon us: Ryan Gosling is making indie rock again. entry.content:
A glorious time is upon us: Ryan Gosling is making indie rock again. All the way back in 2009, Gosling got together with a guy named Zach Shields, and the two of them bonded over the shared experience of getting scared on Disney's Haunted Mansion ride. They started making music together under the name Dead Man's Bones, and they released one very cool album of eerie, folky music, with backing vocals from the Silverlake Conservatory Children's Choir. They played a few live shows around Halloween 2009, too. Now, as the prophecy foretold a few days ago, Dead Man's Bones are back with their first new song in 17 years.

In the time since Dead Man's Bones released their self-titled debut, Ryan Gosling has become an even bigger movie star, while Zach Shields has established himself as a Hollywood screenwriter, working on some of the recent American Godzilla movies and the forthcoming Weapons prequel Gladys. In interviews, Gosling has played it coy on the subject of whether Dead Man's Bones could ever return, and the announcement of their resurrection came as the best kind of surprise. Today, they release a brand new single called "Lost In The Night."

As of right now, we don't know whether "Lost In The Night" is a one-off or whether it's destined to become part of some larger project. It's good, though! Gosling and Shields have evidently done strong work in keeping this secret, since it has evidently been in the works for a while. According to a press release, the two band members attempted to record at "several Los Angeles studios without finding the sound they wanted." Instead, they found their best results when they "took two guitars, two drum machines, and two synthesizers to a farm outside the city and recorded the song in a day."

This time around there's no children's choir on the track, and its sound doesn't have a whole lot of Arcade Fire in its DNA. Instead, "Lost In The Night" is reverb-heavy, atmospheric goth-rock with just the slightest hint of rockabilly in its guitar lines. (A press release names Bruce Springsteen and Suicide as touchpoints, and I also hear distant traces of the Cure.) Ryan Gosling murmurs his lead vocal through a ton of echo, but you can still tell that it's him. The mix includes a simple synth-preset backbeat, some nice harmonies, a few glassy synths, and the kind of breathless backup vocals that I generally associate with '80s horror movies. Throughout, we hear the chirp of crickets. Also, the accompanying press photo has Gosling as a Frankenstein and Shields as a Wolfman, which is fun.

There's a music video, too, but Ryan Gosling and Zach Shields aren't in it, or else they're hidden way in the background. (The clip also doesn't have a director's credit.) Instead, the black-and-white video follows the story of a young couple who start out in an above-ground graveyard — I can't tell if it's New Orleans or somewhere in Europe — before going on a romantic and not-especially-gothy nighttime adventure. Our leads are Noah Jupe, who played one of the kids in the first two Quiet Place movies, and Rain Spencer, star of The Summer I Turned Pretty and the indie drama Good Girl Jane. They're cute together. Check it out below.

"Lost In The Night" is out now on Anti-.

entry.title: Back To Black Turns 20
entry.summary: When Amy Winehouse won Record Of The Year for “Rehab” at the 2008 Grammys, she was visibly stunned. Footage still circulates, her face frozen in pure shock. entry.content:
• Island
  • 2006

When Amy Winehouse won Record Of The Year for "Rehab" at the 2008 Grammys, she was visibly stunned. Footage still circulates, her face frozen in pure shock. She had won five awards that night. Her friend Juliette Ashby turned to her and told her she was proud of her. "Jules," Winehouse replied, "this is so boring without drugs."

The singer’s short life was littered with tragedy, but that disillusioned moment encapsulates the darkness she inhabited. She had just achieved international success with her second album, Back To Black, which came out 20 years ago today in her native UK. (It would arrive in the US about five months later.) Recognition couldn’t save Winehouse — in fact, it could only accelerate her plunge as she endured scrutiny and mockery. She was only 23, yet sang soulfully with the skill, cleverness, and pain of someone who’s lived a thousand lives. She always came off as bigger than herself, an instantly distinguishable cultural icon with her trademark black beehive, huge eyeliner wing, and Monroe piercing.

Frank, Winehouse’s debut LP, was released in 2003, establishing her as an unapologetic, rebellious star in the making. For Back To Black, Winehouse secured Mark Ronson, the hip-hop DJ and rising producer known for bringing a modern touch to retro soul. Also in the mix were the Dap-Kings, the backing band for funk and soul revivalist Sharon Jones, and Frank collaborator Salaam Remi.

The record was cleaner, more focused, and had the hits. Traces of the youthful playfulness from Frank lingered, but her voice was staggeringly more developed and mature, her lyrical subjects more harrowing. Winehouse communicates her gnawing troubles with commanding coolness, her contralto unfurling effortlessly over the band's jazzy exuberance. Nothing about “Rehab,” a song about refusing help, indicates defeat or sadness. The timeless tune — a certified dive bar classic — feels like a victorious march into the abyss. 

“I can express myself,” Amy Winehouse told UK magazine The List in 2007. “I’m not an idiot. I’m not frightened of appearing vulnerable. I write songs about stuff that I can’t really get past personally — and then I write a song about it and I feel better.”

It was easy for many critics to dismiss Winehouse — a messy public figure showing up to performances drunk, getting booed off the stage, and throwing punches at fans who groped her — as an idiot. But her self-destruction was self-aware, chronicled in her music like she was watching herself wreak havoc from afar. When she warns that she’s trouble on "You Know I’m No Good," she’s also warning herself. She sings with complete control about having no control. She’s accepted her ill fate and is doing the only thing she can — turning it all into emotional songs that make time stop. Back To Black is both an exploration of the darkness and an escape from it.

“Wake Up Alone” is a slow number that flirts with doo-wop and feels like pacing through an empty house on a hungover day. Winehouse's voice soars dejectedly, following introspective threads about excruciating heartache caused by a man who’s always keeping her waiting. She sings of trying to keep herself distracted and being flooded with dread. On “Unholy War,” she expresses love in terms of death, like a relationship is a suicide pact. She casually fantasizes about her man reading her will. The influence of girl groups shines through in the soft vocalizing of background singers, providing a melancholy, old-timey backdrop.

One of the most chipper tracks is about crying. On “Tears Dry On Their Own,” Winehouse sounds more clear-eyed than ever, questioning her behavior from an objective perspective, unable to reconcile her feelings with reality: "I don’t know why I got so attached/ It’s my responsibility/ And you don’t owe nothing to me/ But to walk away, I have no capacity." She sings confidently, sounding like the most independent woman in the world, lamenting her inclination for codependency. 

After two decades, there’s never been another Amy Winehouse. The only modern figure who compares is Lana Del Rey, who indulges more in alternative pop than soul, funk, and jazz like Winehouse. Elizabeth Grant had a similar arc of singing in clubs before making it big; but when she did make it big, she crafted a Winehouse-like persona instead of being herself. Her mythos is intriguing, but Winehouse was the real thing. Fiona Apple, whose own rise to fame preceded Winehouse's, could be considered a peer, as she was always unabashedly herself and struggling to handle the spotlight. But these days Apple is constantly disappearing, incapable of existing in the public eye or at least unwilling to bear it.

This much hasn't changed: The music business is not an environment that nurtures women like Amy Winehouse. Even if you grapple with your self-destruction in your art, you will be criticized and harassed for exhibiting that same behavior in your life, especially as a woman. You’re expected to be a role model for young girls and the art comes second.

Though Winehouse’s worst moments often overshadow her accomplishments, the best of her lives on in Back To Black. Her wisdom, her talent, her perspicacity, her tenderness. On the title track, you can hear her own disappointment with herself and her actions, as if she could see her own destiny laid out before her and couldn’t do anything to change it.

After she died of alcohol poisoning in 2011 at age 27, the mocking persisted, even though she wasn’t alive to defend herself. How I Met Your Mother actor Neil Patrick Harris hosted a Halloween party with a meat and cheese buffet platter called The Corpse of Amy Winehouse, a disturbing recreation of her dead body. There’s not a more apt example of the disrespect and hatred Winehouse dealt with just for making art as a troubled woman. But Back To Black stands forever as a triumph, a brilliant artist bravely choosing ultimate vulnerability in a world full of cowards.

entry.content:
The Flaming Lips announced a new album today, the long-awaited follow-up to 2020's American Head. The Teardrop Throbs is out in January, and it marks two important transitions for the band. For one thing, it's coming out on Jack White's Third Man Records, making it their first album since 1990's In A Priest Driven Ambulance not to be released by Warner. Not only is this the Lips' first indie album in 37 years, it's their first without core member Steven Drozd since 1992's Hit To Death In The Future Head.

Drozd joined the Lips as a drummer in 1991, evolving into a multi-instrumentalist and a crucial architect of their music alongside founder and frontman Wayne Coyne. He left the band in 2024 under contentious circumstances, with Coyne claiming he quit and Drozd alleging he was fired. In an interview with Stereogum this year, Drozd told his side of the story, explaining that when he left for addiction treatment, Coyne opted to continue band activities without him: "I went back to treatment. And he just stopped talking to me. That was it. That was me basically being fired from the group. So, you know, I didn’t leave. I was fired. I guess you could say I left because I’m the one that went to treatment, you know what I mean, and didn’t play the shows that were coming up." Drozd has been working on his solo debut album.

Recommended

  • Q&A

    “It’s Strange To Be Talking About the Flaming Lips In The Past Tense”: An Interview With Steven Drozd

    By Zach Schonfeld
    May 6, 2026

The lead single from The Teardrop Throbs is out today. It's called "God Will Control The Werewolves." Along with Coyne, band members Matthew Kirksey and Derek Brown are credited as songwriters, as is Taylor Johnson, who co-produced the new album with Dave Fridmann and Scott Booker (with additional production by Jon Fridmann and Mike Fridmann). It's a psych-pop ballad with shades of The Soft Bulletin, especially when the soaring strings intersect with fuzzed-out lead guitar.

Coyne shared this statement explaining that the lyrics were inspired by an adventure with his young sons under the moonlight:

"God Will Control the Werewolves" started as a little story about my 2 boys (Bloom and Rex) and me playing hide and seek at the park as it was getting dark outside.

We had all become very aware of the moon cycles when we stayed at an ocean view Airbnb about a month previous. The full moon had sucked all the water out of this ocean cove area and we walked a quarter mile out in the seabed seeing strange ocean creatures attached to the rocks.. but yes.. because of the moon we had this amazing adventure so it was fresh in our minds and on this evening of hide and seek it was luckily another full moon.. Bloom asked me if, while him and Rex were hiding, the werewolves would get them (they had also watched a few werewolf movies and knew that the full moon was the time when the werewolves were out and about) and I told him God would control the werewolves for a little bit while we played hide n seek..

The way I heard the song sounding (in my head) was kind of Pink Floyd Dark Side Of The Moon BUT Syd Barrett is still in the band.. ha..

Coyne recently took the stage with longtime collaborator Miley Cyrus at the Hollywood Bowl. Yoshimi fans, please note that the new album also has a song called "Ego Tripping At The Gates Of Hell Part Two." While you await that one, hear "God Will Control The Werewolves" below.

Taste For The Unsavory was made with co-producer Rodrigo Avendaño (Soccer Mommy) and arrives early next year. Other contributors include Mastodon's Bill Kelliher and Preoccupations' Matthew Flegel. entry.content:
The National have always been game for campaigning on behalf of the Democratic Party, especially in their native Ohio. Among other efforts, the band famously lent their Boxer opener "Fake Empire" to Barack Obama's presidential campaign in 2008, and they played a benefit show for Obama's 2012 campaign in Columbus. Now two members of the band are throwing their efforts behind Dr. Amy Acton's campaign for governor and Sherrod Brown's effort to get back in the US Senate.

Lead singer Matt Berninger and multi-instrumentalist/producer Aaron Dessner have signed on for a rally in their Cincinnati hometown. The location of the Fighting For Ohio Rally has not yet been disclosed, but it will be this Wednesday, Oct. 28 from 6:30-8:30 p.m. ET somewhere in Cincy. A ticket signup link is available here.

Acton, who served as Ohio's director of health during the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic, is running against Republican candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who recently faced fervent bipartisan condemnation for an ad featuring Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur.

Acton says she hasn't spoken to Arthur since she was 12, when Acton was removed from her mother's custody after her stepfather was arrested and charged with raping her. Arthur, who defended her husband against the claims, is seen in the ad calling Acton a liar and urging Ohioans not to vote for her. The ad drew strong criticism from both sides of the aisle, including from Ohio's current Republican governor Mike DeWine, who said Ramaswamy should pull it from circulation. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, compared the ad to "hitting pay dirt" and urged Ramaswamy to keep airing it.

Berninger and Dessner aren't the only prominent Ohio natives stumping for Acton. Springfield native John Legend will appear with Acton in Dayton today. Legend, also a longtime supporter of Democrats in Ohio and beyond, is not expected to perform at the Dayton event, according to the Dayton Daily News.

entry.title: Peter Gabriel – “Who Are We Talking To?”
entry.summary: Last Friday, the arch pop duo Haute & Freddy released their cover of Peter Gabriel’s 1986 classic “In Your Eyes.” The cover came out after Mike Flanagan had already used it in the prom scene of his Amazon Prime miniseries Carrie, evoking all kinds of teen-cinema memories in the process. Forty years after the release…
entry.content:
Last Friday, the arch pop duo Haute & Freddy released their cover of Peter Gabriel's 1986 classic "In Your Eyes." The cover came out after Mike Flanagan had already used it in the prom scene of his Amazon Prime miniseries Carrie, evoking all kinds of teen-cinema memories in the process. Forty years after the release of "In Your Eyes," Gabriel remains very culturally present, even as he continues to unveil his new album o\i, one song at a time.

This year, Gabriel is releasing one o\i track every month, unveiling it on the night of a full moon. Last month, Gabriel shared "Face The Wall," the 10th advance single from the LP, and he unveiled the release details a few weeks ago. Now, Gabriel has another new song the itchy and purposeful six-minute chant "Who Are We Talking To?" In a press release, Gabriel says that it was inspired by Marvin Gaye, Fela Kuti, and Curtis Mayfield and that he hopes it encourages some kind of collective action:

"Who Are We Talking To?" was conceived as something that might encourage activism. It might be naive, but I still believe that people have real power for change if they can get together in large enough numbers. Politicians will respond — democracy or not.

My hope is that we start thinking of ourselves as global citizens and that we work together to bring about change on a global scale. These issues that we're looking at, whether it's climate change, AI, pandemics… these are all things that can’t be effectively dealt with on a national level — only globally. A country can have all the bright intentions that it wants, but it's pretty meaningless unless we have everyone working on it at the same time.

Many people feel powerless, oppressed ,and scared at the increasing divisions in the world. At the same time, I would argue that those all-powerful nations that think they are invincible are actually totally vulnerable now. Everybody's hackable. I think we're learning that with the right AI, and once we get quantum computing cutting through cyber security, we're all open to attack and the only sensible course of action would, of course, be to work together.

I really want to see big popular movements that are not about dividing us, with immigration, into them and us, but just the whole messy mass of humanity working together to deal with the things that may very well destroy us soon if we don't. So, this song is a plea for activism.

There is some sort of message, but it's got to be served on a danceable platter. Absolutely the references are from funk and soul and people like Marvin Gaye, Fela Kuti, and Curtis Mayfield creating beautiful rhythmic vehicles to deliver their message. There's a lot from that history that fed into this. We have Leo Nocentelli again on guitar, adding his unique corner of funk to some of these grooves. David Rhodes originally did a really nice funky pattern that we've also integrated. I asked Mike Elizondo to have a go with the Dark-Side mix on this one, and I think he's done a great job.

Just has he has done with every other song from o\i , Gabriel has selected a piece of artwork to go along with "Who Are We Talking To?" In this case, it's "Bloques," from the Spanish artist Juan Genovés. Here's what Gabriel says about it:

The artwork this month is by a Spanish artist called Juan Genovés and this piece "Bloques." When I saw it, I felt it hit the spot. Somehow, like many of the images across the album, it beautifully illustrates some of the ideas within the music. His thoughts on political oppression and resistance show lots of little people standing against these big geometric environments.

I imagine the title "Bloques" refers to these big physical blocks within the painting that seem to represent the barriers that divide people and make it harder for them to come together. I think he believed that these blocks were a power, a force, which could be employed for good or for evil — so appropriate for this song.

Hear "Who Are We Talking To?" below.

o\i is out 11/27 on Gabriel's own Real World label.

entry.content:
In February 2023, Chris Brown reportedly attacked the music producer Abraham Diaw at London's Tape nightclub. Police accused Brown of hitting Diaw with a tequila bottle twice while Omololu Akinlolu, the Florida rapper and vocal coach known as HoodyBaby, punched him. Police called it a "vicious and unprovoked assault," claiming that the two continued to assault Diaw while he tried to flee the club. Now, Brown has been given a suspended eight-month sentence. He will avoid jail time.

Manchester police arrested Brown last year, and he pleaded guilty to one point of affray in July. As Variety reports, Judge Tony Baumgartner addressed Brown at his sentencing: "I take account of your employment and long-established career in music. Your fame, commercial success, and professional standing do not entitle you to special treatment. The law applies equally to everyone." HoodyBaby, who also pleaded guilty, got a four-month sentence, suspended for 12 months.

Brown and HoodyBaby also faced charges of grievous body harm, but those charges were dropped. Earlier this year, Brown went on a successful co-headlining stadium tour with Usher.

entry.title: Turnstile’s Washington Monument Show Was A Sight To Behold
entry.summary: By this point, I’ve seen the Brendan Yates speaker-stack leap so many times, from so many angles. In the middle of Turnstile’s giant free Saturday-afternoon show on the National Mall in Washington, DC, Yates climbed up on a speaker stack that put him maybe seven or eight feet above the stage. As the band launched…
entry.content:
By this point, I've seen the Brendan Yates speaker-stack leap so many times, from so many angles. In the middle of Turnstile's giant free Saturday-afternoon show on the National Mall in Washington, DC, Yates climbed up on a speaker stack that put him maybe seven or eight feet above the stage. As the band launched into "Sunshower," one of the more directly old-school hardcore ragers from last year's Never Enough, Yates launched himself off, curling himself into cannonball position and keeping that form until the split-second before he landed. It looked cool as hell in the moment, and it looked even cooler when captured as a still photograph. When he's in the air, frozen forever before that sea of people, Yates looks like he's about to soar through the sky like Neo at the end of The Matrix.

To anyone who has seen a Turnstile show, Yates' big jump was not a surprise. He does stuff like that all the time. All five Turnstile members are athletes. I've seen drummer Daniel Fang bust out the resistance bands while winding down after a set. Yates doesn't say much between songs, but Turnstile sets are marathons of physical expression. He never stops running, jumping, whirling. None of them do. It's powerful spectacle, and it sweeps you up. You see what they do, and you want to be a part of it. Eight years ago, at a church hall less that three miles away from the Washington Monument, I saw Yates pull off the most impressive stagedive I have ever seen in my life, a front-flip during the first song of their set at the Time & Space record-release show. The rotation, the hang-time — it was astonishing. Yates couldn't do anything like that on Saturday. The days of no-barricade Turnstile shows are over. They're just too big for that now. But that big jump was even more dramatic, in its own way.

Something like 60,000 people came out to see Turnstile play at the Washington monument on Saturday. That's the number that Hassan Wadi, global director of the Canadian relief organization Human Concern International, announced when he introduced Turnstile. It definitely sounds plausible. That's a stadium-sized crowd. Turnstile's set took place in a penned-in area of the National Mall, and it reportedly reached capacity before the show started, but thousands of other people seemingly watched from the hill leading up to the Monument. I've seen some people describe Turnstile set as the biggest non-festival hardcore show in history, and that sounds right to me, though I have no idea how you measure anything like that. The scale of the thing was baffling. I can't believe it actually happened.

How did it happen, anyway? I feel like I need to know. This show was my first time back in Washington, DC since Donald Trump installed a seemingly-permanent National Guard occupation. Police were all over the show, some on horseback. Helicopters buzzed overhead. I cannot imagine the bureaucratic hoops that Turnstile had to jump through to make this show happen, and I can't imagine how many people would've loved to prevent it from taking place. When Turnstile announced the show a few weeks ago, I truly doubted that it would really happen. But no, there was Brendan Yates, waving a Palestinian flag onstage, within sight of the White House. This all goes down at a weird convergence moment when Turnstile are a legitimate pop-culture presence and the current fascist administration is in a defensive crouch, waiting to get mopped up in the midterms. Maybe they just couldn't stop it.

The show was a fundraiser, not a protest, and I'm not naïve enough to think that it represents any kind of tipping point. (The money that it raised was real — up to $261,000 at press time — and I would encourage you to donate any extra money you have to donate to those relief efforts.) Instead, it feels more like Turnstile snuck one past the refs — like the people who would've dedicated themselves to disallowing this event were otherwise occupied. Lots of stuff was happening in DC that day. At the same time, the Chainsmokers were headlining something called the GLOW Block Party outside the Capitol, and you could hear the beats when you were leaving the Turnstile show. Maybe it was just one more mass-gathering event in a city where mass-gathering events happen all the time. Maybe curious onlookers just came though, donated a couple of bucks if they felt like it, and then went about their days. But the sheer scale of what Turnstile accomplished almost didn't feel real.

When Turnstile tour, they go to great lengths to make the crowd feel like they're in it. As a hardcore band headlining gigantic stages, they're in a basically unprecedented situation, and they've put serious work into imagining how that presentation should work. The legendary skate photographer Atiba Jefferson is heavily involved in their video production. They play in front of a huge screen, and most of the time, that screen shows real-time footage of the people in the crowd, not the band. No matter where you look, you see humanity. In DC, they didn't have that. Instead, it was just Turnstile on the same rainbow-striped stage that they used when they played a free show in a Baltimore park when Never Enough came out last year. That show, seemingly staged guerrilla-style, drew an estimated 10,000 people, with no barrier and stagedives all day long. The DC show couldn't be that. The security state had to be involved. But presented without frills or openers or screens, the show still felt like an expression of community.

That community runs deep. Just southeast of the Washington Monument, there's an amphitheater called the Sylvan Theater; it mostly hosts the US Military Band and an annual performance of the 1812 Overture. Fugazi played that venue for the first time in 1993, when most of the members of Turnstile were little kids and guitarist Meg Mills was a few years away from being born. Fugazi's set was in honor of the 30th anniversary of Martin Luther King's March On Washington — King once spoke at the Sylvan Theater, too — and something like 5,000 people came out to see Fugazi. I wasn't one of them, but images of that show captured my imagination when I was a kid. Luckily, Fugazi played a lot of free shows in DC, and I got to see them a few times. Their annual sets at Fort Reno Park felt like overwhelming events as they were happening, even if they never even approached the scale of the Turnstile gig on Saturday.

As Zachary Lipez points out, Pat Graham, the guy who took the above photo of the Brendan Yates speaker-stack jump, also shot Fugazi's 1993 set at the Sylvan. Ian MacKaye was at the Turnstile show, too. I didn't see him in the crowd, but he looks happy in the pictures I've seen. (I did see Justice Tripp, from Trapped Under Ice and Angel Du$t, in the crowd, and I can tell you that he was extremely stoked.) Here's some trivia: MacKaye was one of the kids stagediving in Studio 8H when Fear became the scariest punk band ever to play Saturday Night Live. Turnstile, who just played SNL, are not scary at all. Neither is MacKaye. Scariness isn't the point anymore, if it ever really was.

I don't know if I felt like I was taking part in an historic event on Saturday. It was more of a fun way to spend a beautiful day in a place that we, the American people, supposedly own. The vast crowd didn't seem to fit any real category. I saw parents with little kids on their shoulders, teenage skateboarders, fists-up metalheads, greying retired moshers, guys in banana costumes. (On the way out, I pointed to my End It shirt and tried to joke to one of the banana guys that we're natural enemies. He didn't think it was funny. Maybe my delivery was off.) At least one Chainsmoker was there, too. Afterwards, I got Vietnamese food with a couple of guys who played in Richmond punk bands back in the '90s, and they both brought their middle school-aged kids, who seemed like they had fun. One of them said that he'd always wanted to take his daughter to a hardcore show. (I wanted to bring my kids, too, but they didn't feel like making the trip from Charlottesville to DC, and I don't blame them. Driving into DC sucks.)

I don't want to sentimentalize or gush over the show itself, but it was extremely fun. Turnstile played a version of the Never Enough set that I've seen them play a few times now, and they played it well. They threw themselves around with abandon, bringing joy and energy and bounce and swagger to those gigantic riffs and those catchy, dreamy choruses. Brendan Yates' mic cut out a few times. He got the whole crowd to back up a few times to keep anyone from getting too smushed up front. I love that band and those songs, and I moshed a tiny bit at the end, but I never got lost in the show the way I have with that band in the past. This was not a mosh-to-survive situation. It was a pleasant afternoon with some great music.

But maybe that's just how it happens. Maybe Fugazi's 1993 Washington Monument show felt like a pleasant afternoon with some great music. Maybe the day's victory was symbolic, more than anything. Ever since the Turnstile show ended, my entire feed has been full of videos and photos from the set, and they all look incredible. Get used to seeing that picture of Brendan Yates frozen in the air, seemingly hovering just above the pointy tip of the Washington Monument. That jump wasn't necessarily a statement or a readymade iconic moment. Yates simply did the kind of thing that he does at every Turnstile show. But whatever it comes to symbolize, the image is going to stick with us for a long time.

entry.title: The Weeknd Debuts New Song “Hong Kong” In Hong Kong
entry.summary: Earlier this year, the Weeknd debuted a new song, reportedly titled “Rio,” while performing in Rio, and he premiered another one that seems to be called “Tokyo” while performing in Tokyo last month. On Saturday, the Weekend kicked off a sold-out four-night run at Hong Kong’s Kai Tak Stadium. There, he debuted another brand new…
entry.content:
Earlier this year, the Weeknd debuted a new song, reportedly titled "Rio," while performing in Rio, and he premiered another one that seems to be called "Tokyo" while performing in Tokyo last month. On Saturday, the Weekend kicked off a sold-out four-night run at Hong Kong's Kai Tak Stadium. There, he debuted another brand new song, and you will not be shocked to learn that it's called "Hong Kong."

As captured in the Weekend's social-media video, "Hong Kong" is a grand, dramatic ballad built on a sample of "Seasonal Wind," a 1993 Cantopop ballad from the Hong Kong star Faye Wong. To some of us, Faye Wong will always be best-known as the star of Wong Kar-Wai's classic 1994 film Chunking Express, and that definitely seems to be what the Weeknd had in mind with that sample choice.

The Weeknd's social media video of his "Hong Kong" performance is one static camera angle, far away from the stage, and you can barely see the guy most of the time. Instead, what you see is the totality of the massive screen behind him. It's all footage of Hong Kong, shot by videographer Evan Larsen, that explicitly evokes scenes from Hong Kong films.

Larsen tells the South China Morning Post, "The Weeknd is a massive movie fan and loves Hong Kong cinema from the late ’80s and the early ’90s. He gave me a list of movies to check out before I arrived to get inspired by the city before I saw it in person. That definitely helped, and we wanted to lean into that. " Larsen names Chungking Express and its spiritual sequel Fallen Angels as influences, as well as John Woo's A Better Tomorrow and Hard-Boiled. Great movies!

Larsen says that he has gotten tons of messages from people who remember Hong Kong in the '80s and '90s: "It brought tears to their eyes. Reading these messages is exactly what we are going for... [The Weekend] really wanted to make the song but also the video a full-on love letter to the city. It’s amazing to see that it’s connected with so many people." Watch the performance below.

The Weeknd's last album, 2025's Hurry Up Tomorrow, had songs called "São Paulo" and "Niagara Falls." He's turning into the Mountain Goats with these place-name song titles.

entry.title: A$AP Rocky Accused Of Plagiarizing Part Of AI-Assisted “Shroom Clouds” Video
entry.summary: The road to A$AP Rocky’s Don’t Be Dumb was long and bumpy, and that’s continuing with the rollout for a presumed deluxe edition. Way back in 2021, Rocky previewed a song called “Mushroom Clouds.” On Oct. 19, that song re-emerged as “Shroom Clouds,” a new single with reggie and Jeremih expected to appear on an…
entry.content:
The road to A$AP Rocky's Don't Be Dumb was long and bumpy, and that's continuing with the rollout for a presumed deluxe edition.

Way back in 2021, Rocky previewed a song called "Mushroom Clouds." On Oct. 19, that song re-emerged as "Shroom Clouds," a new single with reggie and Jeremih expected to appear on an upcoming deluxe edition of Don't Be Dumb. A police car in the "Shroom Clouds" video says "30 Oct 2026," so fans think Disc 2 will drop this Friday.

Directed by Rocky plus Aisultan Seitov and Pietro Biz Biasia, "Shroom Clouds" is a surreal video with various callbacks to Rocky's story, like a mural of A$AP Yams and a “Purple Swag” callback. It also uses some AI effects, and now it's being accused of using AI to rip off a small creator. Specifically, fans are flagging the psychedelic tunnel imagery at the 2m25s mark, suggesting Rocky fed someone else's work into AI and inserted himself:

Rocky is accused of ripping off a visual from a 2019 video series using GoPro Fusion directed by Ari Fararooy and Cache Bunny, with visual effects by Cache Bunny, featuring German parkour athlete Jason Paul. It does look remarkably similar, and Fararooy's original Instagram post now has a lot of comments tagging Rocky.

Cache Bunny brought the similarity to light in a series of Instagram Stories over the weekend. "They took our video without permission (or even asking), then fed it into AI and changed Jason to ASAP Rocky," he wrote. "They left our original grass and shadow intact, so this is indisputably stolen ?." After pointing out some more specifics about the alleged thievery, Cache Bunny shared this message:

I've gotten over 600 messages about this so far. I don't know what to do about it yet, but clearly this has struck a major chord with the creator community, which is nice to see. Stealing artists work is not ok, and that's not the precedent we want to set. I can't understand why they didn't just reach out to license the clip, or make their own version inspired by it.

If anyone has advice on what to do please let me know ?

Among the long list of people in the YouTube credits are "AI Artist: Spike and Red" and "AI Artist: Ces," so AI was apparently used in some respect. Fans on Rocky's subreddit already disliked the AI effects before Rocky was accused of theft. Now they are extra disappointed.

A few days before the "Shroom Clouds" video dropped, Rocky shared his thoughts on AI in music in an interview with Complex:

It depends. I feel like when guys like Flexin’ Phoenix [Fenix Flexin], whatever his name is, and Tyga — I don’t know their process of how they make it, but I know when they made it, they caught a lot of backlash and shit like that.

Me, personally, I prefer to do things myself, practically. Say if there's a song that's already out from, say, Kanye [West’s] Graduation. Let's say “Good Morning,” you want to take Kanye's lyrics off, but you want the instrumental, not that you can't just find the instrumental online, but say it was hard to find the instrumental, what you could easily do is use AI to split the stems and take away his vocals so that you could actually rap on it.

AI has a lot of negative connotations. I don't think when it's used in certain ways that it's necessarily a right or wrong thing.

AI is supposed to be a tool in that sense. If somebody does a totally AI-generated song where all they did was prompt something, then I think that that's their thing. But who am I to say what's standard and what's not?

I'm just doing me out here and I'm doing my music practically — the right way. I'm really tapping with musicians, producers, beat makers, just to convey my sound and develop my sound.

Check out Cache Bunny's IG stories below. And kids, if you're thinking about using AI to generate any part of your music video, don't be dumb.

entry.content:
You may have heard Jay-Z chose himself to headline the Super Bowl Halftime Show. Though we're still awaiting official word from the NFL, it's all but confirmed, and it will represent the culmination of a year-long victory-lap campaign celebrating his own legacy. Jigga's been spending this year performing a handful of shows in massive venues, intentionally surveying the full scope of his career. He warmed up by headlining Philadelphia's Roots Picnic in May, then played three huge summer shows at Yankee Stadium — one devoted to the 30th anniversary of debut album Reasonable Doubt, one celebrating 25 years of The Blueprint, and one catchall greatest hits night.

He's since done two shows in London and one in Paris, and the festivities moved on to LA for two JAŸ-Z 30 gigs at Inglewood's SoFi Stadium over the weekend. At Friday's show, he brought out his daughter Blue Ivy for two songs, Scarface for two songs, and DJ Khaled and John Legend for the show-closing "GOD DID." On Saturday, the star power went up to a different wattage, as Snoop Dogg and Dr. Dre took the stage for a five-song mid-show medley. These are all filthy rich old men now, but all these years later, associates of 2Pac and Biggie joining forces like that still feels borderline unbelievable.

In the lead-up to the SoFi shows, screenshots circulating on social media indicated there were plenty of seats available, and Ticketmaster/Live Nation was moving them for prices ranging from cheap to free. The alleged ticket situation was fuel for the skeptics who believe Jay isn't a worthy Super Bowl performer (a crazy take if you ask me, but I can report from experience that these people/bots are legion on Elon Musk's internet). At the very least, it suggests Jay doesn't have the same pull on the West Coast that he enjoys in his home city. At the end of the show, Jay shared some words about that:

People will tell you that nobody was in here tonight, but you got eyes. You can see. People will tell you that the music wasn't great, but you got ears. You gotta understand. You gotta question everything in this world of AI and everything. I mean, it's been going on forever, right? We called it propaganda before. But now, with technology it's caught up. 'Cause people can trick — a lot of tricknology, it's called artificial intelligence because it's mimicking you guys. It's mimicking us. We got real intelligence, not artificial intelligence. We feel, right? This concert tonight, we felt. When Snoop and Dre came out, we felt that shit, correct? Too $hort, Bay Area. Make sure you question everything you feel. Machines are learning you. You tell 'em your swag, you tell 'em your name, and then it mimics you. It can't be you. It could never be you. Question everything, especially in these days and age, this day and age. Y'all feel me? Y'all feel me? Y'all feel me? They will tell you that Jigga ain't Jigga. Hov is motherfuckin' Hov! Peace and love, Los Angeles! I love you!

Is he saying the Ticketmaster screenshots were AI? That he's the victim of a propaganda campaign to make him look washed? I'm not sure I totally follow his line of reasoning, but I do believe he put on two great shows this weekend. Below, check out Jay-Z's speech, some of the guest appearances, and the ticket screenshots that were going around.

entry.content:
May 14, 2022

  • STAYED AT #1:1 Week

In The Number Ones, I'm reviewing every single #1 single in the history of the Billboard Hot 100, starting with the chart's beginning, in 1958, and working my way up into the present. The column is now biweekly, alternating with The Alternative Number Ones on Mondays. Book Bonus Beat: The Number Ones: Twenty Chart-Topping Hits That Reveal the History of Pop Music.

In 2024, Drake went into the fight of his life, and he was demoralized right from jump. His feelings were hurt. Drake's feelings were often hurt. This was nothing new. He might be the most feelings-hurt rap star in history. Drake spent years mining his own hurt feelings for gold, and he usually found it. But this time, he faced massed forces that didn't care about his feelings. Suddenly, half of rap's A-list was arrayed against him. It was a "20 v. one," as he put it. Drake's real enemy in that moment, the one who he truly had to worry about, was past and future Number Ones artist Kendrick Lamar. But when Drake launched his first volley in that feud, his opening words didn't have anything to do with Kendrick. Here's how Drake started things off: "I could never be nobody number one fan/ Your first number one, I had to put it in your hand." He was talking to Future, and he was talking about "Wait For U."

Does Drake have actual friends? I'm sure he does. He has remained tight with the small Toronto crew that came up with him, and a lot of those guys seem to have prominent roles in his various business interests to this day. Drake also forged long collaborative relationships with a bunch of his rap peers, but that always seemed like a series of mutually advantageous business arrangements, less like real love. In that 2024 moment, all of Drake's foes were his former collaborators. But for whatever reason, Future was the one whose participation hurt his feelings the most. Future, the codeine-fogged hedonist prince of Atlanta trap, wasn't the type to get involved in rap feuds, and he and Drake went way back together. If even he was mad at Drake, things must've been really fucked up.

Drake had been in rap feuds before. He hadn't always won them — Pusha T powerbomed him through the ring — but those public back-and-forths hadn't hurt his bottom line. Drake's tone toward Kendrick on his genuinely underrated 2024 diss track "Push Ups" was dismissively condescending, but when he talked to Future, he sounded sad. When Drake said that Future owed him his Hot 100 fortunes, he attempted to big-dog Future, but he also wanted to remind Future that they'd done important things together. His first number one! That's a big deal! ("Push Ups" peaked at #17.)

The Drake/Future relationship was never quite as simple as "your first number one, I had to put it in your hand." In 2021, Drake's not-great quasi-novelty song "Way 2 Sexy" debuted at #1. Future and his friend Young Thug were both on that song. Thug had been on a couple of Hot 100 chart-toppers before that, but Future never had. He'd gotten close. Future's pretty boring Drake collab "Life Is Good," for instance, peaked at #2 in 2020. (It's a 5.) Drake didn't put "Way 2 Sexy" into Future's hand. Instead, that song was a Future track that found its way to Drake. Future never bothered to tell Drake, "Your ninth number one, I had to put it in your hand." Maybe it wouldn't have had the same impact.

Less than a year after "Way 2 Sexy," Future and Drake were back on top of the Hot 100, and this time Future was the lead artist. After all those years as a cultural force whose crossover tracks didn't quite have what it took to conquer the pop charts, Future continued to gain commercial steam even as his music lost its heavy, compelling nihilism and circled the diminishing-returns drain. That was the Drake effect. Before the Kendrick Lamar beef, Drake could release any old shit and still debut atop the Hot 100 without breaking a sweat. Sometimes, his friends benefited from that situation, even if they didn't necessarily appreciate it.

Drake didn't put "Wait For U" in Future's hand, either. Instead, it's another "Way 2 Sexy" situation — an unfinished Future idea getting a little bit of that commercial Drake pixie dust at a time when the Drake pixie dust absolutely did not guarantee a good song. That's the story here — two increasingly uninspired superstars continuing to rack up hits without having to work for it, one guy's resentment toward the other still buried under the surface. Too bad that situation is more compelling than the song itself.

Before we get any further, can we talk about this song title? "Wait For U." I hate it. It's so lazy. My big issue is that Future didn't call it either "Wait For You" or "Wait 4 U." Pick one! Are we writing song titles in text-message speak or actual words? You can't do both. You need to commit. Maybe that title is a signal that "Wait For U" is a song about the refusal to commit, but that's giving it too much credit. It's just one more halfassed slapdash thing about a halfassed slapdash song.

Like so many songs that have appeared in this column recently, "Wait For U" has way too many credited writers and producers. Its main sonic architect seems to be Jacob Denzal Canady, the producer known professionally as ATL Jacob. ATL Jacob was just 21 when "Wait For U" debuted at #1, but he'd already been working in Future's orbit for a few years. As the name implies, ATL Jacob is an Atlanta native. He played in marching band in middle school, and he started making beats around the same time that he started high school. When he was still a kid, he worked as a recording engineer, and he met Future just before he went to prom. Jacob's first beats appeared on Future projects in 2017. In 2019, he produced a bunch of tracks on Future's album The Wizrd, including "First Off," a Travis Scott collab that peaked at #47.

ATL Jacob continues to specialize in the kind of instrumental tracks that attract Future — melodic, echoing Atlanta trap dirges, often with a sinister edge. His work with Future led him to produce for other artists like Young Thug, Roddy Ricch, and Lil Yachty. He made the "Wait For U" beat about a year before it came out, and he gave it to Future, but he didn't think that Future was actually interested. When Jacob thought about pitching that beat to other artists, Future told him not to let anyone else touch it. Jacob told Complex, "[Future] said he listened to that beat every day for a month straight, without rapping or nothing. He was just listening to the beat like it was a song."

The "Wait For U" beat was a song, or at least a sample of a song. The Nigerian singer Tems is listed as a featured artist on "Wait For U," but she doesn't actually sing on the track. Instead, it's built on a sample of "Higher," a track that Tems released in 2020. That feature credit must've taken some backroom negotiation. Whenever someone gets that credit just for being sampled, it feels fake and weird. In this case, though, the sample probably is the best thing about the song. And anyway, it means we get to talk about Tems. Let's do that now.

Temilade Openiyi spent a little bit of time in the UK as a little girl, but she mostly grew up in the Nigerian metropolis of Lagos. (When Tems was born, Bryan Adams' "Have You Ever Really Loved A Woman" was the #1 song in America. If anyone can point me to a Nigerian chart archive so I can figure what was at #1 over there, don't be shy.) Her first name comes from the Yoruba phrase for "the crown is mine," which is cool. She sang in her school choir and wrote her own songs as a kid, and she fell in love with the pirated CDs of American pop and R&B that she got from her brother's friends. But her family didn't consider music to be a real career.

Tems' mother, a doctor, convinced her to study economics at Monash University College in Johannesburg. While she was at school, Tems taught herself how to produce music through YouTube tutorials. After school, she found a job in digital marketing but quit because she wanted to make music. Later on, she told The New York Times, "I just thought, 'This is what I’m actually gifted at. I should do something that comes naturally to me rather than trying to force it.'" Once she started making music, things happened quickly.

Tems put out "Mr Rebel," her first single, in 2018. A year later, she released "Try Me," a tough and determined song that found an enthusiastic audience in Nigeria. This was during the boom times for Afrobeats, the slinky Nigerian sound that pulls in Western influences like American R&B and Jamaican dancehall. Another Tems single, "Damages," was a top-10 Nigerian hit in 2020. More importantly, "Try Me" earned Tems the attention of Wizkid, the Afrobeats star who has already been in this column for appearing on Drake's "One Dance." (Drake's first number one, Wizkid had to put it in his hands.)

In 2020, Tems appeared in Wizkid's track "Essence," which became an international hit. A year later, Justin Bieber, someone who has been in this column many times, jumped on an "Essence" remix. The Bieber remix gave a big boost to both "Essence" and Tems herself. The remix reached #9 on the Hot 100, and Tems joined figures like Burna Boy and Davido on the short list of Afrobeats stars who were marketed hard across the world. (The "Essence" remix is a 7.) Around the same time, Tems appeared on Drake's song "Fountains," a Certified Lover Boy deep cut that peaked at #26.

Tems didn't actually have to do anything on "Wait For U." It was just a matter of ATL Jacob sampling "Higher," a song from Tems' 2020 debut EP For Broken Ears — a young producer from one Black musical tradition latching onto a track from a young performer who comes from a different but vageuly adjacent Black musical tradition. Jacob probably didn't actually sample the studio version of "Higher" but a live-performance video of Tems singing her song over nothing but guitar. He took her pained chorus — "I will wait for you, for you" — looping it and messing with its speed. The murmuring, crystalline loop of that guitar is probably just as important to "Wait For U" as the sound of Tems' voice. Jacob put the standard trap 808 drums and bass-hits on the "Higher" sample, and that's the beat that Future listened to on repeat, like it was a song.

Lots of people ended up with production and songwriting credit on "Wait For U." ATL Jacob might've made the original beat, but he's not the only one with his name on the track. Tejiri Akpoghene, the Nigerian producer who made "Higher" with Tems, gets co-producer credit. So do FnZ, the Australian duo who have already been in this column for their work on the Kid Laroi and Justin Bieber's "Stay." The producer Israel Fowobaje, aka 1SRAEL, has a credit, too. He's a member of Working On Dying, the Philly-based rap production collective, and an occasional Kanye West collaborator. Also credited is the Dallas-born Don Toliver collaborator known as Sonic Major. I don't know what any of these people did on the "Wait For U" beat. It just seems to be one of those things where a half-dozen producers need to tweak a Drake song before the public gets to hear it.

"Wait For U" isn't officially a Drake song, and it didn't start out as a Drake song, but it still has that numbingly sleek Drake gloss on it. I haven't seen any information about how Drake ended up on "Wait For U," but he was a frequent Future collaborator who was into that Afrobeats sound, so it wasn't exactly surprising to hear him on there. That's the thing: There's nothing surprising about "Wait For U." It's the sound of two dominant superstars getting tired and winding down, their music continuing to dominate the charts even as their vitality fades into the mist of memory.

Man, I just don't like this song. It has things that I should like. I was always into the contrast between Drake and Future's voices — one low and grainy, the other sleekly nasal — and that contrast remains, even if the ideas that once animated it are exhausted. The beat itself is pretty enough, though it doesn't particularly stand out. I like what ATL Jacob and his, what, six co-producers do with the acoustic guitar from the Tems track. If "Wait For U" was just a replacement-level Future/Drake collab, I wouldn't love it, but I wouldn't mind it, either. I guess what gets on my nerves is the song's bored, sulky, unexamined notion of romantic love.

Drake and Future sing-rap about different situations on "Wait For U," but neither of them has too much to say about what they've got going on. Future is always high and always on the road, and he's talking to a girl who wants to get closer to him even though he's "in the field like the children of the corn." But the two of them can't even talk because their brains are so fogged that emotions only emerge in dim outlines: "I get more vulnerable when I do pills/ When you drunk, you tell me exactly how you feel." He could genuinely feel awful about their continual communication breakdowns, or he could be manipulating her for sympathy. Either way, the effect is the same, and he keeps her at arm's length.

Drake on the other hand, wants to lavish affection on someone without making any commitment to that person because he's more interested in traveling and making money. He's mad because she's hooking up with someone else, though he doesn't say that he's being exclusive, either. A common Drake theme emerges. He says that he's buying expensive stuff for this girl, and he's disappointed that she still gets mad at him. He's so condescending: "Girl, put a muzzle on it, all that barkin' over dinner/ I was fuckin' with you when you had the tiny Presidential/ You got better when you met me, and that ain't coincidental/ Tried to bring the best out you, guess I'm not that influential/ Guess I'm not the one that's meant for you." It's like he's trying to dump her and guilt-trip her at the same time. I cannot sympathize with one word of this.

Future and Drake shot the fake-medieval Game Of Thrones-ass "Wait For U" video with the rap-video auteur formerly known as Little X. (He has been Director X for a long time now, but I can't stop thinking of him as Little X.) A lot of money clearly went into it, but it's pretty stupid. Future is "the Toxic King," and he leaves his queen behind so he can go fight on a fiery battlefield, though he's also in a bedroom with a bunch of girls in sexy Ren faire outfits. Drake is a knight in shining armor who rides a horse and swordfights some guys to protect a fair maiden. Tems never shows up. I guess some guy betrays Future? And he dumps the queen at the end? The video ends with almost a full minute of credits, but if it came out today, I'd probably assume it was at least partially AI-generated.

"Wait For U" came into the world on Future's album I Never Liked You, which is mostly decent, at least as far as late-period autopilot Future albums go. It's probably not a great sign when the artist is asleep on the record cover, though at least his sleep mask matches his suit. Future's previous releases hadn't generated that much heat, and he and his label invested resources into pulling in big guest stars and turning the album release into an event.

Drake is on two I Never Liked You tracks. The other one was "I'm On One," which has nothing to do with the 2011 DJ Khaled hit with the exact same title, even though Drake was on that song, too. The Future/Drake "I'm On One" is a little more spirited than "Wait For U," anyway. Past and future Number Ones artist Kanye West showed up on "Keep It Burnin" and shot a video for the song with Future, though it was during the time when West always wore those blank masks in public. ("I'm In One" peaked at #11, "Keep It Burnin" at #15.)

The week after I Never Liked You came out, all 16 of its tracks appeared on the Hot 100, four of them in the top 10. "Puffin On Zootiez," the album's second-biggest single, peaked at #5, and I like that one. That's Future in eerie-banger mode, which is always my favorite Future mode. (It's a 7.) "Wait For U" debuted at #1 during the period that Harry Styles' "As It Was" was in and out of the top spot. As you'd probably expect, the song fell from the top spot after one week. As you might not expect, however, "Wait For U" lingered. It's not one of these incredible disappearing #1 songs. The song parked itself in the top 10 for months, and it stayed on the Hot 100 for almost a year. Today, I Never Liked You is double platinum, and the "Wait For U" single is platinum 11 times over.

Why were so many people drawn to "Wait For U"? Why are so many people still apparently drawn to "Wait For U," given that song some of Future's biggest Spotify numbers? I have no idea. In any case, it was a big moment for Tems, though she still hasn't transitioned into a different level of global stardom. Tems' biggest chart moments all came alongside established Western superstars, and most of them happened in 2022. A few months after "Wait For U," Tems appeared alongside Grace Jones on past and future Number Ones artist Beyoncé's excellent album track "Move," which peaked at #55. Later in the year, Tems co-write and sang backup on Rihanna's "Lift Me Up," her soundtrack song from the Black Panther sequel Wakanda Forever. It briefly looked like that song might signal a Rihanna comeback, but that obviously didn't happen. ("Lift Me Up" peaked at #2. It's a 4.) As lead artist, Tems is currently having her biggest-ever chart success. This week, her song "What You Need" is at #29, and it appears to be on the way up.

I Never Liked You was a successful record that showed Future in a prolonged creative stasis, but that wouldn't last forever. Later in 2022, Future showed up on future Number Ones artist Metro Boomin's "Superheroes (Heroes & Villains)," which also features Chris Brown, someone who's been in this column a few times. Chris Brown's only barely on it, though, and not in the video version at all. Mostly, it's Future over his old friend Metro's most cinematic production, sounding generally more animated than he did on anyone else's tracks at the time. ("Superheroes (Heroes & Villains)" peaked at #8. It's an 8.)

That "Superheroes" song was on Metro Boomin's Heroes & Villains album, and some not-that-interesting complications with its release and its Grammy fortunes led to a rift between Metro and Drake, a guy who had already rapped on plenty of Metro beats. Eventually, Future apparently got sick of Drake, too. A couple of years after "Wait For U," Future had a few pointed lines that seemed aimed at Drake, and he and Metro also released the song where Kendrick Lamar went public with his long-simmering anti-Drizzy vendetta. But we'll get to that song in a future column. Or a Future column. You know what I'm saying. A future Future column.

Future and Drake eventually made up. That's a relief, right? You were worried, I can tell. Earlier this year, Future appeared on Drake's resentful sulk "Ran To Atlanta," a years-late riposte to another song that'll eventually appear in this column. Future and (especially) Drake both sounded reinvigorated on "Ran To Atlanta," and that song peaked at #2. (It's an 8.)

As for Drake, we're nowhere near done with him yet. He'll be back in this column very soon.

GRADE: 3/10
